content: Sucralfate is a medication prescribed primarily for the treatment of ulcers. It works by adhering to the damaged ulcer tissue, forming a protective barrier against stomach acid and digestive enzymes, which facilitates the healing process. In some cases, it may be prescribed for other conditions. If you have questions about its use for other purposes, consult your doctor or pharmacist. Sucralfate is available in tablet and liquid forms and is taken orally. It is typically administered four times a day: one hour before meals and at bedtime. It should be taken on an empty stomach, either two hours after or one hour before eating. Follow the instructions on your prescription label carefully, and ask your doctor or pharmacist if you have any questions. Take the medication exactly as directed, without altering the dose or frequency. Shake the liquid form well before measuring your dose. For optimal effectiveness, sucralfate must be taken regularly, and it may take up to eight weeks for ulcers to heal. In addition to treating ulcers, sucralfate is sometimes used to protect the stomach lining in patients taking aspirin or to manage mouth sores caused by cancer chemotherapy. Discuss the potential risks and benefits of using this medication for your specific condition with your doctor. Before starting sucralfate, inform your doctor and pharmacist if you are allergic to it or any other medications. Provide a complete list of all prescription and nonprescription medications you are taking, especially antacids (e.g., Mylanta, Maalox), anticoagulants (e.g., warfarin), certain antibiotics (e.g., ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin, tetracycline), digoxin, phenytoin, quinidine, and vitamins. If you are taking any of these, avoid taking them within two hours of sucralfate. Additionally, inform your doctor if you have a history of heart or kidney disease or diabetes. If you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding, notify your doctor. If you become pregnant while taking sucralfate, contact your doctor immediately. If you miss a dose of sucralfate, take it as soon as you remember. However, if it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and continue with your regular schedule. Do not take a double dose to compensate for a missed one. Sucralfate may cause mild side effects such as constipation, abdominal pain, and gas. To minimize these effects, consume a high-fiber diet (including fruits, vegetables, salads, and bran) and drink plenty of fluids. Severe side effects are rare but may include passing red or black stools or vomiting material that is bright red or resembles coffee grounds. If you experience any of these symptoms, contact your doctor immediately. Serious side effects can be reported to the FDA’s MedWatch Adverse Event Reporting program online or by phone. Store sucralfate in its original container, tightly closed, and out of reach of children. Keep it at room temperature, away from excessive heat and moisture (do not store it in the bathroom). Dispose of expired or unneeded medication properly, and consult your pharmacist for guidance on disposal. Keep all appointments with your doctor and laboratory, as certain tests may be required to monitor your response to sucralfate. Do not share this medication with others. If you have questions about refilling your prescription, consult your pharmacist.
